title: Review: Chromosomes, karyotypes and genome organization; Recombinant DNA and genetic modification; DNA replication; DNA replication detail (deeper); Translation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: GR06a#t3 term and clue written for the game; GR06a#t4 term and clue written for the game; CD05a#t2 term and clue written for the game; GE01a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CD05a#N.8, GE01a#N.2b, GE01b#N.7, GE02#N.11, GE05a#N.4, GR06a#N.10b, CD05a#N.4b, GE01a#N.6b, GE01b#N.10, GE05a#N.10, GE01a#N.4b, GE05a#N.7. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Transformation
items.clue: Uptake of a plasmid by host cells; only a small fraction of them manage it.

items.label: Universal genetic code
items.clue: Reason any host cell builds the same polypeptide from transferred human DNA.

items.label: Eukaryotes
items.clue: Organisms that keep most of their DNA in a nucleus, as several linear chromosomes

items.label: Helicase
items.clue: Enzyme that unwinds DNA and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.

questions.stem: Each chromatid of human chromosome 1 contains one DNA molecule about 85 mm long. When the cell divides, the condensed chromosome is about 10 µm long (illustrative round value). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The DNA is about 8.5 times longer than the chromosome, because it is wound round histones and coiled further.
The DNA is about 8 500 times longer than the chromosome, because it is wound round histones and coiled further.
The DNA is about 8 500 times longer than the chromosome, because packing removes bases to shorten the molecule.
The DNA is about 8 500 times longer than the chromosome, because the double helix twists tighter with no proteins involved.

questions.stem: Before a eukaryotic cell divides by mitosis, all of its DNA is replicated. Which statement best explains how this replication maintains the continuity of hereditary information from the parent cell to its two daughter cells?

options.text: It doubles the amount of DNA, and each daughter cell then receives half of the parent cell's genes.
It makes a second complete copy of the DNA, so each daughter cell receives a full set of the parent's genes.
It keeps each original DNA molecule intact and makes an all-new copy for the other daughter cell.
It builds each new strand as an identical copy of the strand it pairs with, so no information changes.

questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA molecule in which both strands contain only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) is replicated three times in a medium that supplies only light nitrogen (¹⁴N), producing 8 DNA molecules. How many of the 8 DNA molecules contain any ¹⁵N?

options.text: 1 of 8
8 of 8
2 of 8
4 of 8

questions.explanation: In round 1 the two ¹⁵N strands separate and each pairs with a new ¹⁴N strand. They stay intact in every later round, so after round 3, 2 molecules contain ¹⁵N and 6 contain only ¹⁴N.

questions.stem: A hypothetical species of bacterium has a mutation that makes its DNA ligase inactive at 40 °C but not at 30 °C. Cells are moved from 30 °C to 40 °C just before a round of DNA replication begins. Which prediction about the new DNA made at 40 °C is correct?

options.text: Each leading strand would be continuous, but each lagging strand would stay as separate fragments.
Both new strands would be complete, but they would not stay paired with their template strands.
Neither new strand would be made, because nucleotides could not be linked to the growing strands.
The lagging-strand fragments would still be joined into one strand, though more slowly than at 30 °C.

questions.stem: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?

options.text: It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.
It carries the mRNA bases that the ribosome converts into the amino acids of the polypeptide.

questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.

questions.stem: Bacteria were transformed with a plasmid carrying a version of a human gene that contains no introns. The transformed bacteria made a polypeptide with the same amino acid sequence as the human polypeptide. Which explanation best relates this result to a larger biological concept?

options.text: The plasmid carried the human polypeptide itself, which the bacteria took up
Transformation changed the bacteria into human-like cells able to make human proteins
The plasmid DNA built the polypeptide directly, without being transcribed or translated
Bacteria and humans share the genetic code, so the gene's codons specify the same amino acids

questions.stem: A line of eukaryotic cells grown in a laboratory carries a mutation that greatly reduces the amount of histone protein the cells make. Which prediction about the DNA in the nuclei of these cells is best supported?

options.text: Its DNA will be less tightly packed, so its chromosomes will be less condensed.
Its DNA will have a changed base sequence, as histones set the order of its bases.
Its two DNA strands will come apart, as histones hold the base pairs together.
Its chromosomes will lose some genes, as histones are sections of the DNA.

questions.explanation: Histones are the proteins that DNA winds around to become condensed. With far fewer histones, less DNA can be wound and packed, so the chromosomes are expected to be less condensed.

questions.stem: In a cell of a hypothetical species of animal, DNA replication has produced a chromosome made of two sister chromatids. Which statement correctly describes the DNA of the two sister chromatids?

options.text: Both carry the same base sequence, but only one of them contains DNA from the original molecule.
Each carries half of the chromosome's genes, so the two together hold one full set of genes.
Each original strand acted as a template, so each chromatid has one original strand and one new strand.
Each is one strand of the original DNA molecule, so the two have complementary sequences.

questions.stem: The experiment is run in reverse. Bacteria are grown for many generations on light nitrogen (¹⁴N), then moved to a medium containing only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N). Replication is semi-conservative. What will the DNA show after two generations on ¹⁵N?

options.text: Two bands of equal amount: intermediate and light.
Two bands of equal amount: intermediate and heavy.
One band, between intermediate and heavy.
Two bands: one quarter light, three quarters heavy.

questions.explanation: Generation 1: every molecule is one light + one heavy strand (intermediate). Generation 2: 4 molecules, 2 hybrids holding the old light strands and 2 all-heavy.

questions.stem: The coding region of an mRNA, from the first nucleotide of the start codon to the last nucleotide of the stop codon, is 903 nucleotides long. How many amino acids does the polypeptide translated from this region contain?
questions.explanation: 903 ÷ 3 = 301 codons. AUG codes for methionine and the stop codon codes for nothing, so the polypeptide has 301 − 1 = 300 amino acids.

questions.stem: A drug binds to the helicase of a hypothetical species of bacterium and stops it from working; the other replication enzymes are not affected. Which prediction about DNA replication in cells treated with the drug, and the reason for it, is correct?

options.text: Replication would stop, because helicase is what adds nucleotides to the new strands.
Replication would continue, because topoisomerase would separate the parental strands.
Replication would stop, because the parental strands would no longer be separated.
Replication would continue more slowly, as the parental strands would come apart unaided.

questions.stem: An antibiotic stops the ribosome from moving along the mRNA but does not affect the binding of tRNAs or the formation of peptide bonds. What effect will this have on translation of an mRNA?

options.text: Only the first peptide bond forms, since the next codon cannot be moved into place for a tRNA to bind.
Translation is unaffected, because all the tRNAs bind along the mRNA before any peptide bonds are formed.
Translation is unaffected, because each tRNA leaves the ribosome before the next one binds to the mRNA.
The chain still grows, because each tRNA stays attached to its amino acid and the next tRNA simply joins onto it.
